idiom_name: Next.js route-segment cache (export const revalidate = ...) or Cache-Control in front
implementation_notes: On a typed Node stack there is no separate page-cache call to make: in Next.js the full-route cache is declared per route segment with export const revalidate = 300 (false caches until purged, 0 forces dynamic rendering) and invalidated on demand with revalidatePath/revalidateTag, while the framework decides what is prerendered because a route that reads cookies()/headers() opts out of static caching. Outside a framework the realization is the HTTP contract: express the response in Cache-Control/s-maxage, Vary and ETag types, and put the bytes in a CDN or reverse proxy. Prefer the framework route when the page is a route and freshness can be expressed as a revalidation window; prefer the header route when the cache must outlive the process or be shared by non-Next services.
pitfalls: Reading cookies()/headers() - or a fetch with no-store - silently makes the whole route dynamic: nothing is cached and the only symptom is miss traffic on every request.
revalidate is a route-segment value and the smallest one wins, so one child with a short window forces the parent layout to re-render too; reason about purges route-wise, not file-wise.
Putting user-specific output into a statically cached route is a data-protection defect, not a performance choice - vary, or opt the route out.
